body_markdown:
## **TL;DR**


- For SaaS co-marketing, sponsorship, referral, or combined programs, start with the[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) and select the applicable terms.
- If you are forming a legal partnership, reselling a product, or building a deep integration, ask counsel which paperwork you need instead.
- Define each party’s deliverables, referral qualifications, fees, deadlines, and end date before seeking approval.
- Have legal, finance, and marketing review relevant terms. Confirm the final version, then obtain signatures from authorized representatives of both companies.
- Store the signed agreement and track payment triggers and expiration. This guide is educational, not legal advice.


## **What a SaaS partnership agreement actually covers**


A SaaS partnership agreement records a commercial collaboration between two existing companies. The word “partner” often describes a go-to-market relationship, such as promoting each other’s products or sending sales leads. A general or limited partnership is a different legal arrangement involving shared ownership or operation of a business. If you intend to form one, ask counsel about entity-formation documents rather than using a go-to-market template.


The commercial agreement can cover several kinds of programs. In co-marketing, the companies might run a joint webinar. In sponsorship, one company might pay for placement at the other’s event. In a referral program, one company sends prospective customers to the other under agreed qualification and payment rules. A combined program can include more than one of these activities in the same deal. The[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) provides a starting point for documenting that kind of collaboration, while the companies still need to agree on their specific commitments.


A reseller relationship, in which one company sells the other’s product, may need different terms. A technical integration may also require separate paperwork covering access and responsibilities. Identify those arrangements before choosing a template, and involve counsel when the proposed relationship goes beyond promotion or referrals.


## **Choosing the right agreement: a selection matrix**


Choose paperwork based on what each company will do and what it will receive in return. For a commercial go-to-market program, the[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) can be a starting point. If the deal creates a new entity, gives one company responsibility for selling the other’s product, or requires substantial technical or data-sharing commitments, ask counsel what additional agreement you need.


**Deal type** **Trigger to look for** **Starting point**


Co-marketing Both companies agree to promote each other through a webinar, campaign, or shared content. Use a partnership agreement to specify deliverables, approvals, and timing.


Sponsorship One company pays for placement in the other’s event, newsletter, or content. Use a partnership agreement to define the placement, fee, and cancellation terms.


Referral One company introduces potential customers and receives a fee for qualifying deals. Use a partnership agreement to define a qualified referral, attribution, and payment trigger.


Combined program The companies pair promotions with paid referrals or sponsorship. Use one agreement if each activity and its payment terms can be stated clearly.


Entity formation The companies plan to share ownership or issue equity in a new venture. Seek counsel for entity-formation documents rather than using a go-to-market agreement.


Reselling One company will sell, contract for, or support the other’s product for customers. Seek a reseller agreement that addresses customer obligations and commercial terms.


Integration or API partnership The companies plan deep product integration or substantial customer-data processing. Seek specialized terms and review whether a data processing agreement is needed.


Before choosing a template, write down who contracts with the customer, who handles customer data, and how money changes hands. A fixed fee for an accepted introduction differs from an arrangement in which the companies share ongoing product revenue. Those answers help you identify whether a standard commercial partnership agreement fits or whether counsel should shape the paperwork before drafting begins.


## **Defining the deal terms with SaaS examples**


A partnership agreement records what each company will do, but the companies must negotiate the deal details. The[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) provides a Cover Page and applicable Standard Terms, with annotated terms that explain its fields in depth. Check where each negotiated detail belongs rather than assuming a field supplies the answer. The dates, amounts, and criteria below are illustrations, not legal defaults.


For a co-marketing campaign, two SaaS companies might agree to host a webinar for US and Canadian prospects on June 15, 2027. One company provides the speaker and slides, while the other manages registration and sends two promotional emails. The agreement can specify when each company must approve the materials and which registration link records each company’s contribution. If neither company owes a fee, say so. Webinar registrations would not become qualified referrals or earn a payout unless the companies separately agree on those terms. The campaign could expire on June 30 after both companies deliver their registration reports.


For a sponsorship, a SaaS company might pay $2,500 for a partner’s July 2027 newsletter placement aimed at US subscribers. The deal should identify the placement size, publication date, approval deadline, and evidence of delivery. The sponsor could owe payment within 30 days after receiving an invoice and confirmation that the placement ran. A tracked link can measure visits without making payment depend on clicks or qualified referrals. The agreement could expire on July 31, while preserving any unpaid fee obligation.


For a referral program, a SaaS company might pay a partner 10% of the first year’s subscription fees it actually receives from an eligible customer. The companies would need to define an eligible referral, perhaps a US prospect submitted through a shared form before the prospect enters the SaaS company’s sales pipeline. They should also decide who resolves competing claims when two partners submit the same prospect, how quickly the SaaS company confirms acceptance, and whether refunds reduce the payout. A program ending December 31, 2027, could still allow payment for accepted referrals that sign within 60 days after expiration, if both companies choose that rule.


Before either company signs, put each negotiated obligation, payment trigger, territory, and end date in the agreement. A template gives you a place to document the bargain. Neither its fields nor these examples decide the bargain for you.


## **Protecting the brand, data, and internal sign-off**


Before sending a SaaS partnership agreement for signature, confirm what each company may publish and what information it may exchange. For a co-marketing campaign, specify which logos, product names, and customer quotes each party may use, where they may appear, and who approves the final materials. Ask marketing to check the proposed uses against both companies’ brand guidelines. Do not assume that permission to use a logo also covers an endorsement or a customer story.


A referral program needs a defined boundary for customer data. Decide whether the partner will send only a business contact’s name and work email, or whether the program calls for account details or usage data. Limit the shared fields to what the referral requires, and have legal or privacy reviewers check the applicable notices and permissions. If one company will process personal data on the other’s behalf, ask counsel whether a data processing agreement, or DPA, is needed alongside the[partnership agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) . A referral arrangement alone does not answer that question.


Route the draft to the people who own its commitments. Marketing should approve brand uses and campaign deliverables. Finance should check fees, payment triggers, and the budget. Legal should review the agreement and any proposed changes to standard terms. Keep one working copy, assign one person to consolidate redlines, and label each version so reviewers know which draft contains the current deal terms.


Send exceptions such as an unusual liability cap, exclusivity, or permission to resell customer data to counsel rather than settling them in a business-side email thread. Contract workflow software can help route approvals and preserve the document history, but it cannot decide whether those terms are acceptable for your company.


## **Executing the agreement: signatures and countersignatures**


Finalize the[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) before sending it for signature. Check that the Cover Page records the negotiated program, fees, dates, and any other deal-specific terms. Review the applicable Standard Terms alongside it, and confirm that both parties have the same final version. If someone spots an error after routing, stop the signature process and send a corrected version rather than relying on an email clarification.


Each company should name a signer who has authority to commit it to the agreement. The person who negotiated the deal may not have that authority. Check your company’s signing policy, ask the partner to confirm its signer, and involve counsel if authority or a proposed change remains unclear.


Agree on signing order before sending the document. For example, one party can sign first and the other can countersign after confirming that no terms changed. Track both signatures and give each party the fully signed copy. Countersignature provides a clear record of each party’s assent, though whether an agreement is enforceable depends on its terms and applicable law.


A basic e-signature tool collects signatures. Contract workflow software can also route the approved version, show who still needs to sign, and retain an audit history and signed record. Common Paper connects those steps with reusable agreements and internal approvals, but software cannot decide whether unusual terms need legal review.


## **Managing the partnership after signature**


Store the fully signed agreement, including any attachments and signature record, where the partnerships lead and finance can find the current version. Record the effective date, program owner, payment terms, and end date alongside it. If the parties later change a fee or deadline, keep the signed amendment with the original agreement rather than relying on an email thread.


Track referrals against the criteria and payment schedule the parties agreed to. For each lead, record when the partner submitted it, whether it qualified, which customer or deal it relates to, and whether the event that triggers payment occurred. Finance can then check an invoice against the contract before paying it. For co-marketing or sponsorship commitments, track promised deliverables and due dates in the same way.


Set a reminder before any renewal notice deadline, not just the expiration date. The partnerships lead needs time to review results, ask the partner about continuing, and obtain approval for changed terms.[Common Paper](https://commonpaper.com/) supports structured contract data and downstream integrations, which can help carry agreed dates and payment terms into finance or CRM tracking. Whatever tools you use, assign an owner to check those records so missed deliverables and approaching deadlines receive attention.


## **FAQs**


**Does a referral agreement need a separate DPA?** Not automatically. If partners exchange only business contact details, review what data each party receives and how each party uses it. If a partner processes personal data on your behalf, ask counsel whether you need a data processing agreement (DPA) or whether an existing one covers the activity.


**Can one agreement cover co-marketing and referrals?** Yes. A combined program can set out each partner’s marketing deliverables alongside qualified-referral criteria, attribution rules, payment triggers, and end dates. The[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) provides a starting point for that discussion, but both companies still need to agree on the deal terms.


**What if a partner wants exclusivity?** Specify which activities, customers, and territory the restriction covers, how long it lasts, and what happens if the partner misses its commitments. An open-ended promise could limit other partnerships.


**When do we need a reseller agreement instead?** Use specialized paperwork when the partner sells your product to customers, rather than introducing customers who contract with you directly. A reseller arrangement needs clear terms for customer contracts, billing, support, and responsibility for the service.


These answers are intended for general education purposes and do not replace legal advice on a specific deal.


## **Conclusion**


Choose an agreement that matches the deal, then make someone responsible for carrying out its terms. For co-marketing, sponsorship, or referral programs, start with the[Common Paper Partnership Agreement](https://commonpaper.com/standards/partnership-agreement/use-your-partnership-agreement/) . Confirm the deliverables, payment triggers, and end date before authorized signers execute the final version. Store the countersigned agreement and track its obligations so you can run subsequent partnerships without rebuilding the process each time.


Entity formation, reseller rights, unusual data use, and high-stakes terms may require different paperwork and legal counsel. This guide is intended for general educational purposes, not legal advice.
